speech_to_text_content: Chlorine gas is produced in a laboratory experiment. The relative molecular mass of chlorine is 71. Which method should be used to collect this gas? Options are: A) Water displacement, B) Downward delivery, C) Upward delivery, or D) Gas syringe only.

options.option_text: Water displacement
Downward delivery
Upward delivery
Gas syringe only

explanation: The correct answer is B) Downward delivery. Chlorine gas has a relative molecular mass of 71, which is much greater than the relative molecular mass of air (29). This means chlorine is denser than air and will sink downward. In downward delivery, the gas enters from above and sinks into a gas jar, displacing lighter air upward. Water displacement (A) is not suitable because chlorine is very soluble in water and would dissolve rather than being collected as a gas. Upward delivery (C) is for gases less dense than air (like ammonia). A gas syringe (D) alone is not the best method for collecting large volumes of gas.

title: Separating a Salt and Sand Mixture
content:
## Practice Question 3

A student has a mixture of salt and sand. Which sequence of steps would successfully separate both components?
speech_to_text_content: A student has a mixture of salt and sand. Which sequence of steps would successfully separate both components? Options are: A) Sieve the mixture then filter the result, B) Add water to dissolve the salt, filter to separate sand, then evaporate the filtrate, C) Heat the mixture to sublime the salt, or D) Use a separating funnel to separate the components.

options.option_text: Sieve the mixture, then filter the result
Add water to dissolve the salt, filter to separate sand, then evaporate the filtrate
Heat the mixture to sublime the salt
Use a separating funnel to separate the components

explanation: The correct answer is B) Add water to dissolve the salt, filter to separate sand, then evaporate the filtrate. This method works because salt is soluble in water while sand is insoluble. The procedure is: (1) Add water to the mixture - salt dissolves forming a solution, sand remains as solid; (2) Filter - the sand (residue) remains on the filter paper, salt solution (filtrate) passes through; (3) Evaporate the filtrate - heating drives off the water, leaving pure salt crystals. Option A fails because sieving works for different particle sizes, but salt and sand particles may be similar sizes. Option C fails because salt does not sublime - it has a very high melting point. Option D fails because a separating funnel is for liquid-liquid mixtures, not solid mixtures.

title: Separating Two Miscible Liquids
content:
## Practice Question 4

A student has a mixture of two miscible liquids with boiling points of 78°C and 95°C. Why would simple distillation NOT be suitable for this separation?
speech_to_text_content: A student has a mixture of two miscible liquids with boiling points of 78 degrees Celsius and 95 degrees Celsius. Why would simple distillation not be suitable for this separation? Options are: A) The boiling point difference is too large, B) The boiling point difference is too small (only 17 degrees Celsius), C) Miscible liquids cannot be separated by any distillation method, or D) The apparatus is not available.

options.option_text: The boiling point difference is too large
The boiling point difference is too small (only 17°C)
Miscible liquids cannot be separated by any distillation method
The apparatus is not available

explanation: The correct answer is B) The boiling point difference is too small (only 17°C). Simple distillation requires a SIGNIFICANT boiling point difference (typically >25°C) between the two liquids. With only 17°C difference, when the lower-boiling liquid (78°C) evaporates, the higher-boiling liquid (95°C) also evaporates at the same time. This means both liquids enter the condenser together, and you get a mixture rather than pure separation. Fractional distillation (with a fractionating column) would be needed instead. Option A is incorrect because a larger difference would actually be better. Option C is incorrect because miscible liquids can be separated by fractional distillation. Option D is not the reason for the limitation.

title: Interpreting Melting Point Data for Purity
content:
## Practice Question 5

A student measures the melting point of a white solid and finds it melts gradually between 118°C and 125°C. The reference melting point for the pure substance is 122°C. What can be concluded?
speech_to_text_content: A student measures the melting point of a white solid and finds it melts gradually between 118 degrees Celsius and 125 degrees Celsius. The reference melting point for the pure substance is 122 degrees Celsius. What can be concluded? Options are: A) The substance is pure because the melting point is close to the reference value, B) The substance is impure because it melts over a range of temperatures, C) The substance is pure but the measurement was inaccurate, or D) The substance has been contaminated with water.

options.option_text: The substance is pure because the melting point is close to the reference value
The substance is impure because it melts over a range of temperatures
The substance is pure but the measurement was inaccurate
The substance has been contaminated with water

explanation: The correct answer is B) The substance is impure because it melts over a range of temperatures. A pure substance has a sharp melting point at a specific temperature - it melts at one temperature, not over a range. The fact that this substance melts gradually between 118°C and 125°C (a range of 7°C) is a clear sign of impurity. Impurities lower the melting point and cause melting to occur over a range of temperatures. While the centre of the range (121.5°C) is close to the reference value (122°C), the wide range is the key indicator of impurity. Option A is incorrect because the range, not the average value, indicates purity. Option C is incorrect because a pure substance would show a sharp melting point, not a range. Option D is too specific - the impurity could be any substance, not necessarily water.

title: Calculating Rf Values in Chromatography
content:
## Practice Question 6

In a paper chromatography experiment:
- A component travels 4.8 cm from the baseline
- The solvent front travels 8.0 cm from the baseline

Calculate the Rf value for this component.

Rf = _____________ (Give your answer to 2 decimal places)
speech_to_text_content: In a paper chromatography experiment, a component travels 4.8 centimetres from the baseline and the solvent front travels 8.0 centimetres from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value for this component. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
explanation: The correct answer is 0.60. The Rf value is calculated using the formula: Rf = Distance travelled by component / Distance travelled by solvent front. In this case: Rf = 4.8 cm / 8.0 cm = 0.6 = 0.60 (to 2 decimal places). Rf values are always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). An Rf of 0.60 means the component travelled 60% of the distance that the solvent front travelled. This Rf value can then be compared with reference values to identify the component.

title: Explaining Crystallisation vs. Evaporation
content:
## Practice Question 7

A student needs to separate a dissolved salt from water. Explain why crystallisation would produce purer crystals than simple evaporation.

Your answer should include:
- How each method works
- Why one produces purer crystals than the other
- At least one practical difference between the methods
speech_to_text_content: A student needs to separate a dissolved salt from water. Explain why crystallisation would produce purer crystals than simple evaporation. Your answer should include how each method works, why one produces purer crystals than the other, and at least one practical difference between the methods.

answer.answer_text: Model answer: Evaporation works by heating the solution until all water evaporates, leaving salt crystals behind. Crystallisation works by heating the solution until it becomes saturated, then cooling it gradually. Crystallisation produces purer crystals because slow cooling allows salt atoms to arrange in an orderly, crystalline pattern, while impurities remain dissolved in the remaining solution. In evaporation, rapid heating causes fast evaporation, and impurities become trapped within the crystals as they form quickly. Practically, crystallisation takes much longer (requires time for gradual cooling) while evaporation is faster. Crystallisation produces large, well-formed crystals, while evaporation produces small, irregular crystals.

explanation: This question tests understanding of two key separation methods. The model answer should include: (1) Evaporation: heating until all solvent evaporates, leaving dissolved solid behind. (2) Crystallisation: heating to saturation point, then cooling gradually to allow crystals to form. (3) Why crystallisation is purer: slow cooling allows atoms to arrange in orderly patterns, impurities stay in solution and are removed when you filter; in evaporation, impurities can be trapped in crystals as they form rapidly. (4) Practical differences: crystallisation is slower (requires time for cooling), evaporation is faster; crystallisation produces large pure crystals, evaporation produces smaller crystals with more impurities. Students should demonstrate understanding that purity depends on the rate of crystal formation and the separation of impurities.

title: Designing a Separation Procedure
content:
## Practice Question 8

A student has a mixture containing:
- Sand (insoluble in water)
- Salt (soluble in water)
- Iron filings (magnetic)

Design a complete procedure to separate all three components. You should:
1. Identify which separation method to use for each step
2. Explain why each method is suitable
3. Describe the order of steps (which should be done first, second, third)
4. Identify what you would have at the end of each step
speech_to_text_content: A student has a mixture containing sand, salt, and iron filings. Design a complete procedure to separate all three components. You should identify which separation method to use for each step, explain why each method is suitable, describe the order of steps, and identify what you would have at the end of each step.

answer.answer_text: Model answer: Step 1 - Magnetic attraction: Use a magnet to remove iron filings from the mixture. Iron is magnetic while sand and salt are not. This is the easiest and quickest method. After this step, you have separated iron filings. Step 2 - Add water: Add water to the remaining mixture (sand and salt). Salt dissolves in water (forms a solution) while sand is insoluble and remains as a solid. Step 3 - Filtration: Filter the mixture to separate the insoluble sand from the salt solution. The residue on the filter paper is sand. The filtrate (liquid) contains dissolved salt. Step 4 - Evaporation: Heat the salt solution to evaporate all the water, leaving salt crystals behind. Alternative: Crystallisation could be used instead of evaporation to get purer salt crystals. Final products: Iron filings (separated in step 1), sand (separated in step 3), salt (separated in step 4).

explanation: This question tests the ability to design a complete separation procedure using multiple methods. The model answer demonstrates: (1) Correct identification of three methods: magnetic attraction, filtration, and evaporation. (2) Correct order: magnetic attraction first (removes iron), then add water and filter (separates sand), then evaporate (recovers salt). (3) Explanation of why each method works: iron is magnetic, sand is insoluble, salt is soluble. (4) Clear identification of products after each step. Acceptable variations: crystallisation instead of evaporation for salt recovery. Students should show logical thinking about the order of steps (you must remove magnetic iron first before adding water, otherwise the magnet would remove wet iron filings which is messier).
